title: Colleagues
hook: the people at work are your neighbors
tomorrow: what does a good boss owe, and what does a worker owe back?

segments.voice: Yesterday, excellence: the craft voice and the love voice, both Catholic. The line was well done.

A shift goes sideways: the oven's running hot, the line's out the door, and the new person is drowning. Mark tells about four people who once carried a load together. Their friend can't walk. Jesus is teaching in a house in Capernaum, so packed that nobody can get near the door. So the four climb up onto the roof, open it up, and lower their friend down on his mat, one corner each.
screen: `THE NEW PERSON IS DROWNING.` → `A HOUSE TOO PACKED TO ENTER.` → `ONE CORNER EACH.`

segments.voice: Feel that scene for a second. Dust and bits of roof falling on the crowd below. Rope pulling at their palms. Four corners, four people, the weight shifting whenever one of them slips. Then Mark's surprising line, in the Douay-Rheims: "when Jesus had seen their faith." Their faith. The carriers. Before a word is said to the man on the mat, Jesus notices the people holding the corners. Colleagues are a lot like that. Mostly you didn't choose them. You're in the same packed house with the same crowd at the door, and the work only moves when each one takes a corner. Paul gives it to the Galatians as a rule for any community: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." And in Luke, when a lawyer asks Jesus who his neighbor is, the answer is a story about a traveler who stops on the road for a stranger. At work, the neighbor is often the person at the next station. Here's the thing to tell a friend: in Mark, the first faith Jesus sees in this story isn't the sick man's. It's his friends'.
screen: `DUST, ROPE, FOUR CORNERS.` · `JESUS SAW THEIR FAITH.` · `BEAR ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · `THE NEIGHBOR AT THE NEXT STATION.` · then, large: `NEIGHBORS AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Stand and hold your arms out low, as if you had one corner of a mat, and feel the pull in your shoulders. Bring to mind one person you work or study with who's carrying something heavy right now. Hold your corner for them until the bell, and choose one small way to lift some of it.
Colleagues. The people you work beside: neighbors, each holding a corner.
The line to keep: neighbors at work, each one holding a corner of the mat. That's the day, done.

chat.meaning: In Mark, Jesus sees the faith of the four who carried the mat, and Paul says bear one another's burdens. The person at the next station is a neighbor.

Capernaum.meaning: a town on the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught

Galatians.meaning: the churches in Galatia, which Paul wrote to

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older English Catholic translation of the Bible

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 2:5 and Galatians 6:2 quoted from memory; confirm exact Challoner wording ('fulfil' is the translation's spelling).

Mark 2:1–4 paraphrased: the house in Capernaum, no room even at the door, four carriers, the roof opened. Sensory details (dust, rope) are the narrator's imagining, framed as 'feel that scene'; Mark says they uncovered the roof and let down the bed. Confirm the framing.
Galatians 6:5 ('every one shall bear his own burden') sits near 6:2; no game item claims Paul says only one or the other.
